en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga 8.
Pasūrasuttaniddesa
Now he will explain the exposition of the *pasūra* verse:
"They proclaim purity in this very life,
and do not speak of purification through other teachings."
Those who rely on what they call "beauty" therein,
being many and settled in individual truths,
proclaim that purity is found right here.
Right here they speak of, discuss, declare, proclaim, illuminate, and express purification, complete purification, total purification, liberation, complete liberation, and total liberation.

They speak of, discuss, declare, proclaim, illuminate, and express purification, complete purification, total purification, liberation, complete liberation, and total liberation [with the view]: "The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
... "The world is not eternal..."
The world is finite… the world is infinite… the soul and the body are identical…
The soul is one thing and the body another;
the Tathāgata exists after death;
the Tathāgata does not exist after death.
“The Tathāgata exists after death... does not exist after death... both exists and does not exist after death...

neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is vain”—thus they speak of purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, release, and total release; they declare, explain, recite, illuminate, and express it—saying, "Purification is found right here."
“They claim there is no purity in other teachings.
Setting aside their own teacher, the teaching, the assembly, the view, the practice, and the path, they cast asunder, uproot, and surround all rival doctrines:
“That teacher is not omniscient; that teaching is not well-proclaimed; that assembly is not well-practiced; that view is not auspicious.”
"The way of practice is not well-proclaimed; the path does not lead to liberation. Herein there is no purity, nor purification, nor complete purification;
no freedom, nor liberation, nor total liberation. Therein they are not purified, nor cleansed, nor completely cleansed;
they are not freed, nor liberated, nor totally liberated. It is inferior, base, low, wretched, contemptible, and limited."
"They say thus, they speak thus, they discourse thus, they declare thus, they illuminate thus, they express themselves thus:
'Purity is not found in other things;
whatever one relies upon, that alone they call beautiful therein.'"

"Depending on which" means depending on, relying on, clinging to, approaching, adhering to, and being intent upon a certain teacher, the proclamation of Dhamma, a group, a view, a practice, or a path.
"Therein" means by one's own view, by one's own inclination, by one's own preference, and by one's own conviction.

"One who speaks of beauty" means one who speaks of what is beautiful, who speaks of what is splendid, who speaks as a wise man, who speaks firmly, who speaks according to the natural order (*ñāya*), who speaks with reason, who speaks according to characteristics, who speaks according to cause, who speaks according to ground—that is, by one's own conviction.
"Depending on which they speak of beauty therein":
they are settled in various individual truths.
"Various" means many ascetics and brahmins who are settled, established, attached, approached, clinging to, and intent upon various individual truths.
“‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’—thus they are settled, established, attached, committed, clung to, and intent upon it.
‘The world is non-eternal...

[and so on] ...the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false’—thus they are settled, established, attached, committed, clung to, and intent upon it.”
They are settled separately in individual truths.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Right here they proclaim purity.”
They do not speak of purity in other doctrines;
for they rely on what they call beautiful therein,
being settled in various individual truths.
Desiring debate, they plunge into the assembly and burn the fool with their mutual wrangling;
relying on one another, they utter contentious talk.
"Desiring praise, skilled in eloquent speech, they enter the assembly desiring debate. "Desiring debate" means:
they desire debate, they seek debate, they have debate as their aim, they have debate as their purpose, and they wander about searching for debate.

"Having plunged into the assembly": having plunged into, entered into, immersed oneself in, and gone within the assembly of kshatriyas, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, and the assembly of ascetics—it is those who desire debate who plunge into the assembly.
"They strike the fool, each against the other."
Two people who are mutually opponents, two who create quarrels, two who create strife, two who create disputes, two who create legal issues, two who are litigants, two who engage in debate;
they regard, see, look at, observe, contemplate, and examine one another as foolish, inferior, base, low, wretched, contemptible,
and insignificant— thus, "they regard one another as fools."
“They speak of ‘disputing over talk’ (kathojja).

This means they are dependent on, attached to, clinging to, approaching, adhering to, intent upon another teacher, another proclamation of Dhamma, another group, another view, another practice, and another path.
“Disputing over talk” is said to mean quarreling, brawling, strife, contention, and conflict.
Alternatively, "speech-riot" (*kathojja*) means that speech which is full of passion (*anojavantī*).

They speak of strife, they speak of quarreling, they speak of brawling, they speak of contention, they speak of dispute, they speak of turmoil; they talk, they say, they illuminate, they express it—thus, those who depend on others speak of "speech-riot."
"Desiring praise, proponents of what is wholesome.

"Desiring praise" means: desiring praise, seeking praise, having praise as their aim, having praise as their primary concern, wandering about in search of praise. "Proponents of what is wholesome" means:

speakers of the wholesome, speakers of wisdom, speakers of stability, speakers of the method, speakers of cause, speakers of characteristics, speakers of reason, speakers of the proper ground; that is to say, they speak according to their own tenets.
They desire praise and are fond of recounting what is skillful.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Those who desire debate, having entered the assembly...”
Burning one another with folly,
they speak contentious talk, dependent on each other,
desiring praise and proclaiming themselves as virtuous.
One who is fit for discourse in the midst of an assembly,
yet desires praise, becomes frustrated;
but when he is refuted, he becomes dejected.
He becomes angry at censure, seeking out faults.

He is intent on his own talk in the midst of an assembly— whether in an assembly of khattiyas, or an assembly of brahmins, or an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics— being intent, engaged, devoted, committed, associated, and occupied with speaking his own talk.
"Engaged in debate in the midst of an assembly, desiring praise, he becomes a destroyer.
Desiring praise means: desiring, accepting, longing for, yearning for, and craving praise, eulogy, fame, and reputation.
"He becomes frustrated even before the conversation" means that even prior to the discussion, he is full of doubt and frustration, thinking:
"Will I win? Will I lose? How shall I effect a refutation? How shall I make a counter-argument?
How shall I establish a distinction? How shall I establish a further distinction?"
"How shall I make a twist? How shall I make an untwist? How shall I make a cut?
How shall I make a circle?"—thus, even before the conversation has begun, one who is full of doubt and hesitation is struck down;
thus, desiring praise, one is struck down.
"But when he has been refuted, he becomes dejected.
Those who are questioners in the assembly, members of the assembly, or those who frequent the assembly, they carry him off.
They carry him off by way of the meaning, thinking, "What was said has lost its point. They carry him off according to the sense.
Thinking, "It was spoken devoid of phrasing," they take it away from the phrasing;
thinking, "It was spoken devoid of meaning and phrasing," they take it away from both the meaning and the phrasing;
[they say], "The meaning has been wrongly interpreted by you, the phrasing has been wrongly set down by you, the meaning and phrasing have been wrongly interpreted and wrongly set down by you."
"Your refutation was not made; your counter-argument is faulty. Your distinction was not made; your further distinction is faulty.
Your entanglements were not made; your disentangling is faulty. Your cutting off was not made; your circle is faulty.
Your discourse was uneven, poorly composed, ill-spoken, ill-articulated, ill-uttered, and ill-proclaimed," they thus rebuke him.
"But when struck down, he is dejected":
when struck down, he is dejected; he is oppressed, afflicted, diseased, and despondent—thus, "but when struck down, he is dejected."
“He becomes angry at blame, seeking faults”:

he becomes angry, provoked, and settled in resentment at blame, censure, dispraise, and the taking away of reputation; he manifests anger, hatred, and dissatisfaction—thus, “he becomes angry at blame.”
"Randhamesī means one who seeks out faults, one who seeks out transgressions, one who seeks out lapses, one who seeks out failures, one who seeks out errors, one who seeks out vulnerabilities.
He becomes angry at such censure;
thus the Blessed One said.
“One who desires praise in the midst of an assembly becomes frustrated when refuted;
but when his position is overturned, he becomes dejected.”
"He becomes angry at censure, seeking out faults"—
thus do those who investigate questions declare his doctrine to be defeated and refuted.
He laments and grieves, a debater defeated;
he reproaches himself, saying, "He has surpassed me.

Regarding his argument which they call "defeated"—that is, his argument which is inferior, base, fallen away, lost, and not fulfilled—they say this, they speak thus, they declare thus, they illuminate thus, they express it thus.
They say Yama’s argument has been defeated;
those who investigate the question declare it refuted.
Those members of the assembly, the attendants, and the counselors who investigate the question carry it away [in defeat].
They misappropriate it by saying, "It was spoken apart from the meaning," thus misappropriating it from the perspective of the meaning;
they misappropriate it by saying, "It was spoken apart from the phrasing," thus misappropriating it from the perspective of the phrasing;
they misappropriate it by saying, "It was spoken apart from both the meaning and the phrasing," thus misappropriating it from the perspective of both the meaning and the phrasing.
“Your meaning is poorly grasped; your phrasing is poorly set forth; both your meaning and phrasing are poorly grasped and poorly set forth.
You have failed to provide a refutation; your counter-argument is ill-executed. You have failed to establish a distinction; your further distinction is ill-executed.
You have failed to provide a winding-around; your unwinding is ill-executed. You have failed to provide a cutting-off; your circle is ill-executed—this is a discordant discourse.”
"Badly spoken, badly uttered, badly chanted, badly recited, badly articulated"— thus they "take away," meaning they take away [the answer] from those who investigate the question.
He laments and grieves, being one of inferior speech.

"Lamenting" means: "I have directed my attention to one thing, thought of another, reflected on another, and perceived another; that [other] has a great faction, a great assembly, and a great retinue;
yet this assembly is divided and not in harmony;

for the sake of a harmonious assembly, I shall break off this further exchange of conversation"—such speech as this is chaff, idle chatter, lamentation, the act of lamenting, and the state of lamenting.
He laments.
He sorrows: he sorrows thinking, "It is his victory," and he sorrows thinking, "It is my defeat."
He grieves, thinking, "He has gain," he grieves,
thinking, "I have no gain," he grieves, thinking, "He has fame."
He grieves, thinking, "It is my disrepute";
he grieves, thinking, "There is praise for him";
he grieves, thinking, "It is my censure."
He grieves, thinking, "It is his happiness," and he grieves, thinking, "It is my suffering.
He thinks, "He is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated; he is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."

"I am not honored, respected, esteemed, worshipped, or venerated; I do not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, or medicinal requisites for the sick"—thus he sorrows, tires, laments, beats his breast, falls into confusion, and grieves:
this is what is meant by "he laments and sorrows."
"A base doctrine" means a base doctrine, a low doctrine, a deficient doctrine, a doctrine that has been discarded, a doctrine that is not complete—
one who holds such a base doctrine laments and grieves.
"He reproaches [others], saying, 'He has surpassed me.'"
Thus he has surpassed me in debate; he has gone beyond, transcended, overcome, and passed by me.
In this way too, "he has surpassed me.
Or else, having overcome me in debate, having overwhelmed, encompassed, crushed, and subdued me, he moves, dwells, conducts himself, proceeds, protects, maintains, and sustains himself.
"Thus he has surpassed us," they lamented.
"Lamentation" (anutthunā) is said to be empty talk, vain talk, prattle, the act of prattling, and the state of having prattled—
"thus he has surpassed us," they lamented.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“That whose doctrine they say is defeated,
And repudiated by those who investigate questions;”
“He laments and grieves, a speaker of inferior views;
‘He has overstepped,’ he says, reproaching [the opponent].
These disputes have arisen among the ascetics.
Among these, there is the destruction of what has been raised up;
seeing this, one should refrain from contentious speech,
for there is no gain in praise that comes from killing another.
"These disputes have arisen among the recluses.
"Recluses" refers to whoever, outside of this [teaching], has gone forth into homelessness and has entered the life of a wanderer.

These quarrels over views, brawls over views, conflicts over views, disputes over views, and contentions over views have arisen, been produced, come into being, been generated, and become manifest among the recluses.
These disputes have arisen among the recluses.
Regarding these, there is striking and counter-striking; there is victory and defeat.
There is gain and loss;
there is fame and disrepute;
there is blame and praise.
There is pleasure and pain,
there is joy and grief,
there is the agreeable and the disagreeable.
There is attraction and repulsion;
there is the struck-out and the struck-down; there is compliance and opposition.
By victory the mind is uplifted; by defeat the mind is depressed.
By gain the mind is uplifted; by loss the mind is depressed.
By fame the mind is uplifted; by disrepute the mind is depressed.
The mind is uplifted by praise and depressed by blame;
the mind is uplifted by pleasure and depressed by pain;
the mind is uplifted by joy and depressed by grief.
"The mind is uplifted by elevation and depressed by dejection"— in these cases,
there is "uplifting and depressing."
"Having seen this too, one should desist from wrangling.

"Having seen this too" means: having seen, perceived, weighed, scrutinized, analyzed, and made manifest this danger; that is to say, in regard to quarrels over views, disputes over views, conflicts over views, debates over views, and contentions over views—one should desist from wrangling.
Having seen this too, one should desist from wrangling.
"Kathojja" is said to mean quarrel, strife, dispute, contention, and conflict.
Alternatively, "kathojja" refers to talk that is not radiant; one should not engage in such talk, nor should one engage in quarreling.
One should not engage in quarreling,
one should not engage in contention,
and one should not engage in dispute.
One should not create strife;
one should abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence the strife of quarreling, brawling, contention, and dispute.

One should be aloof from, detached from, and fully withdrawn from such strife; one should have emerged from it, escaped it, and be dissociated from it, dwelling with a mind that has transcended its boundaries.
Seeing this too, one should desist from frivolous talk.

For there is no other benefit in killing than the gain of praise—whether it be for one's own welfare, for the welfare of others, for the welfare of both, or for any benefit pertaining to the present life. There is no such thing.
Whether it be a matter pertaining to the future life,
a matter that is superficial,
or a matter that is profound.
Whether it be a hidden meaning, a concealed meaning,
or a meaning that requires further interpretation.
Whether it be a meaningful purpose,
a blameless purpose,
or a purpose free from defilement.
Whether it be the meaning of purification or the ultimate meaning, there is no such thing; they do not exist, they are not found, they are not perceived— thus, "there is no killing,
there is no taking what is not given" is a source of praise and gain.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“These disputes have arisen among the recluses;
in these, there is destruction and ruin.”
"Seeing this as well, one should abstain from frivolous talk;
for one who does not kill, there is gain through praise.
Or rather, one is praised therein.
Having proclaimed his doctrine in the midst of the assembly,
he laughs and exults because of that,
having attained his goal just as he had intended in his mind.
"Or else he is praised therein. "Therein" means:
he is praised, extolled, celebrated, and lauded by his own view, his own inclination, his own preference, and his own doctrine;
thus, "or else he is praised therein."
He proclaims his own doctrine in the midst of an assembly—
whether an assembly of khattiyas, brahmins, householders, or ascetics— having proclaimed and explained it,
having proclaimed and explained the counter-argument, having established it, and having elaborated upon it.
"Having illuminated, having made radiant, having proclaimed, and having grasped—
the dispute in the midst of the assembly—
he laughs and exults because of that."
Thus, through that sense of victory, he is satisfied, elated, joyful, glad, and fulfilled in his intention;
or else, smiling with bared teeth, he laughs and exults because of it.
Thus, by means of that victory, he is "puffed up" (*unnata*); for "puffing up" (*unnama*) is the flagging, the grasping, the desire for a banner of the mind.
"Therefore he laughs and exults because his mind has attained that goal. Having won,
reached, attained, found, and acquired that goal for victory.
"Just as the mind was, just as the mind became, just as the consciousness became, just as the intention became, just as the discernment was"—
having attained that goal, just as the mind was.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
But if he is praised there, having proclaimed his doctrine in the midst of the assembly,
he will laugh and exult because of that.
"Having attained that goal as his mind desired.
That which is his exaltation is a ground for affliction;
indeed, this is called pride and overweening pride.
Having seen this as well, one should not dispute;
for the wise do not say that purity comes through that.
Whatever arrogance there is, that is the ground of his affliction.
That which is inflation, loftiness, a banner, grasping, and the desire for self-display of the mind— that is inflation.
"It is his ground of affliction" means that it is his ground of affliction, ground of injury, ground of oppression, ground of friction, ground of calamity, and ground of misfortune.
Whatever exaltation there is, that is his ground of affliction.
"But he speaks of conceit and overweening conceit":
that person speaks of conceit and speaks of overweening conceit.
"But he speaks with conceit and overweening pride.
Having seen this, one should not engage in dispute.

Having seen this danger, having perceived it, weighed it, scrutinized it, fully understood it, and made it manifest—regarding disputes over views, quarrels over views, conflicts over views, debates over views, and contentions over views.
Having seen this as well, one should not dispute; that is, one should not engage in quarreling, nor engage in brawling, nor engage in contention, nor engage in disputing;
one should not engage in strife. One should abandon, dispel, and eliminate quarreling, brawling, contention, disputing, and strife.
One should bring it to an end, lead it to non-existence;
one should be aloof from, abstain from, refrain from, have emerged from, escaped from, and be dissociated and detached from strife, quarreling, contention, dispute, and wrangling;
one should dwell with a mind that has transcended all boundaries—having seen this, one should not engage in dispute.
"For the skilled do not say that purity comes through that. Here,
"the skilled" refers to those who are skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, skilled in the foundations of mindfulness,
skilled in the right endeavors, skilled in the bases of psychic power, skilled in the faculties, skilled in the powers, skilled in the factors of enlightenment, and skilled in the path.
Those who are skilled in the fruit and skilled in Nibbāna— those skilled ones— do not say, do not speak,
do not declare, do not illuminate, and do not communicate that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, or total release comes through disputes over views,
quarrels over views, conflicts over views, controversies over views, or strife over views.
For the wise do not say that purity comes through that.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Whatever inflation there is, that is its ground of affliction."
But he speaks with pride and arrogance;
having seen this too, one should not engage in dispute,
for the wise do not say that purity is attained thereby.
Just as a hero, when challenged by a king for combat,
rushes forward seeking another hero; so you too,
O hero, flee back to where he is!
"Previously there was nothing for battle.
Like a hero when questioned by the king’s cook.
Here, "hero" means one who is brave, valiant, resolute, fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and one who does not flee.
"Reared by royal food": nourished, fed, brought up, and raised on royal hard foods and royal soft foods—just as a hero is reared by royal food.
"Challenging him": they seek an opponent hero.

Thus, roaring, bellowing, and thundering, he comes, approaches, and draws near, desiring, accepting, longing for, yearning for, and craving a rival hero, a rival man, a rival enemy, and a rival wrestler—thus it is said:
"He roars, approaching while desiring a rival hero.
"Run away by that very path, O heroes! [he says].
"Run away from that very place where that holder of wrong views is; avoid him, go by that way, pass him by—that one is your rival, your opponent, your enemy, your adversary.
"O hero, run away from that very place where he is!
There was never even before this any reason for fighting."
Previously, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, those defilements which were antagonistic,
contrary, thorny, and opposing— those do not exist, they are not present, they are not found, they are not obtained; they have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed,
rendered incapable of arising, burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
That is to say, "he comes for battle"— that is, for the sake of fighting, for the sake of quarreling, for the sake of brawling, for the sake of contention, for the sake of dispute,
for the sake of strife— yet even before that,
there is no such thing as "for battle. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Just as a warrior, when challenged by a king for combat,
charges forward seeking an opponent hero; so you too,
O hero, flee back toward him from whom you came!"
"Even before this, there was none such as Yudhāyā.
Those who grasp at views and dispute,
declaring, "This alone is the truth";
"You yourself should speak thus: 'Indeed, these views do not exist for you,' when a debate has arisen because of those who act as opponents.
Those who, grasping at views, engage in disputes" refers to those who take up one or another of the sixty-two types of speculative views.
Having grasped it, taken hold of it, mastered it, clung to it, and adhered to it, they dispute, engage in quarreling, engage in brawling, engage in contention, and engage in strife, saying:
"You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya; I understand this Dhamma and Vinaya. What do you know about this?"
“You do not understand the Dhamma and Vinaya; you have practiced wrongly, whereas I have practiced rightly. My position is consistent, while yours is inconsistent.
You said later what should have been said earlier, and you said earlier what should have been said later.
Your established practice has been overturned; your argument has been refuted; you are defeated. Go forth to save your argument, or disentangle yourself if you can.”
"Those who, having grasped views, dispute and declare:
'Only this is the truth. They speak, say, utter, illuminate, and express: 'The world is eternal; only this is true, all else is false.'"

“They proclaim, speak, utter, illuminate, and express: ‘The world is eternal’ …pe… ‘A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is false’”—thus they proclaim:
“This alone is the truth.”
"You should speak to them, for there is nothing here that you cannot do;
when a debate has arisen, you are one who can offer a counter-argument.

You should speak to those holders of views, argument against argument, refutation against refutation, rebuttal against rebuttal, distinction against distinction, sub-distinction against sub-distinction, entanglement against entanglement, and unraveling against unraveling.
"Cutting with cutting, encircling with encircling— those who are your rivals, your adversaries, your enemies, and your competitors—
you shall speak against them, for they do not exist here when a debate has arisen and one must act as an opponent."

When a dispute has arisen, come into being, been produced, been fully produced, and become manifest, those who would act as opponents, act contrarily, act like thorns, or act as adversaries—engaging in quarreling, brawling, strife, contention, and conflict—do not exist, do not exist now, are not found, and are not perceived; they have been abandoned... [etc.]
"They have been burnt by the fire of knowledge"—
you should say this to them, for when a debate has arisen, they are unable to offer a counter-argument.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Those who grasp at views and dispute,
saying ‘This alone is the truth,’ you should see them as such; for indeed, there is no truth in them.”
“When a debate has arisen, because of acting as an opponent.
But those who wander about having made enemies of one another,
not contradicting view with view;
Among those, what would you gain, Pasūra,
for those who here have nothing grasped as supreme?
But as for those who wander having become free from enmity—
"Army" refers to Māra’s army. Bodily misconduct is Māra’s army; verbal misconduct is Māra’s army; mental misconduct is Māra’s army; greed is Māra’s army; hatred is Māra’s army;
delusion is Māra’s army; anger … resentment … contempt … insolence … envy … [are Māra’s army].

… stinginess … deceit … guile … obstinacy … hostility … conceit … arrogance … intoxication … negligence … all defilements … all misconduct … all distresses … all fevers … all torments … all unwholesome volitional formations are Māra’s army.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Sensual pleasures are your first army;
the second is called discontent."
... [as before] ... The asura does not conquer him;
having conquered, he indeed attains happiness.

Since, by means of the four noble paths, the entire army of Māra and all the defilements that act as adversaries have been conquered, defeated, broken, shattered, turned away, and put to flight, for that reason it is said, "having disarmed" (*visenikatvā*).
"Yet" (*ye*) refers to the Arahants whose taints are exhausted.
"They move" (*caranti*) means they move about, dwell, conduct themselves, proceed, protect, maintain, and sustain themselves.
But those who wander having separated themselves from views, not contradicting one view with another—
those for whom the sixty-two types of speculative views have been abandoned, utterly cut off, stilled, subsided, and rendered incapable of arising again.
Burnt by the fire of knowledge, they do not conflict view with view, do not oppose it, do not abandon it,
do not strike it down, and do not obstruct it; thus,
"not conflicting view with view" means they do not conflict view with view.
"Among them, what would you find as a match?
means: among those Arahants whose taints are destroyed, what would you find as a counter-hero, a counter-man, a counter-enemy, or a counter-champion?—among them, what would you find as a match?
"There is nothing superior that has been grasped.

For those Arahants whose taints are exhausted, there is nothing—nothing at all—that has been grasped as "this is supreme, foremost, best, distinguished, preeminent, highest, and excellent," nor has it been clung to, adhered to, settled upon, or devotedly fixed upon. There is no such thing.
They do not exist and are not found; they have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, rendered incapable of arising,
and consumed by the fire of knowledge—
for those who here possess nothing as a supreme grasping.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“But those who wander having separated themselves,
not contradicting one view with another view;”
"Among those, what would you gain, Pasūra,
for whom there is nothing here that has been grasped as supreme?
Then you fell into deep reflection.
Mentally brooding over speculative views,
you have met with the Shaken One as an equal;
indeed, you will not be able to travel along with him.
"Now you have come to right reflection.

"Now" (*atha*) refers to the connection of words, the conjunction of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of phonemes, and the sequential order of words; this is what "now" signifies.
"Having come to a state of applied thought": while thinking, reflecting, and intending, [he wonders], "Will there be victory for me? Will there be defeat for me? How shall I effect a refutation?
How shall I effect a rebuttal? How shall I effect a distinction? How shall I effect a further distinction? How shall I effect an entanglement? How?
Thinking, "How shall I untie it? How shall I cut it? How shall I form a circle?"—thus reflecting, pondering, intending, you have come, approached, arrived, and met with me;
thus you came with deliberation.
"Thinking out views with the mind" means:

"mind" refers to that which is *citta*, *mano*, *mānasa*, *hadaya*, *paṇḍara*; it is the mind-base (*manāyatana*), the mind-faculty (*manindriya*), consciousness (*viññāṇa*), the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*), and the corresponding mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
Thinking and reflecting on a view with the mind, such as "the world is eternal," or...
Thinking with the mind of speculative views such as “the world is eternal,” or …pe… “a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.”
"Meet with the one who is cleansed (dhona), for you will not be able to travel together.
Here, "cleansed" refers to wisdom.
That which is wisdom, understanding... [as above] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
For what reason is wisdom called "shaken off"?
Because by means of that wisdom, bodily misconduct is shaken off, washed away, thoroughly cleansed, and completely purified;
and verbal misconduct... [and so forth].
All unwholesome volitional formations have been shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and thoroughly purified.
Alternatively, by right view, wrong view is [shaken off];
by right intention, wrong intention is [shaken off], and so on...
By means of right liberation, wrong liberation is shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified.
Alternatively, by means of the noble eightfold path, all defilements... all misconducts... [are shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified].
All distresses … all fevers … all torments …
All unwholesome volitional formations have been shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and purified by him.

The Blessed One is endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, furnished with, fully furnished with, and equipped with these qualities that shake off; therefore, the Blessed One is "one who has shaken off.
He is one whose passion has been shaken off, whose evil has been shaken off, whose defilements have been shaken off, and whose fevers have been shaken off.
"He cleanses.
"The chariot shall meet with the cleanser; you will not be able to drive it together.

The wanderer Pasūra was not capable of meeting with the Blessed Buddha, the Cleanser, to engage in a contest of wits, to converse, or to enter into a formal discussion by taking up the challenge of a debate.
For what reason?
The wanderer Pasūra is inferior, base, lowly, wretched, fourth-rate, and limited.
But the Blessed One is the foremost, the best, the most distinguished, the leader, the supreme, and the most excellent.
Just as a hare is not capable, when meeting in a direct encounter with a rutting elephant, of seizing the yoke;
just as a jackal is not capable, when meeting in a direct encounter with the lion, the king of beasts, of seizing the yoke;
just as a young calf, still nursing at its mother’s udder, is not capable, when meeting in a direct encounter with a powerful bull, of seizing the yoke.
Just as a hawk is not capable of meeting with a *garuḷa* of the Vainateyya lineage and engaging in a contest of strength to seize him by the neck;
just as an outcaste is not capable of meeting with a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and engaging in a contest of strength to seize him by the neck;
just as a dust-demon (*paṃsupisāca*) is not capable of meeting with Indra, the king of the gods, and engaging in a contest of strength to seize him by the neck; [so too is this person].
In the same way, the wanderer Pasūra is not capable of meeting with the polished Buddha, the Blessed One, to engage in a contest of wits, to converse, or to enter into a discussion.
Why is that? Because the wanderer Pasūra is of inferior wisdom, of base wisdom, of low wisdom, of poor wisdom, of mediocre wisdom, and of limited wisdom.
For the Blessed One is one of great wisdom, of broad wisdom, of smiling wisdom, of swift wisdom, of sharp wisdom, of penetrative wisdom;
he is skilled in the classification of wisdom, possessed of manifold knowledge, and has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

He has reached the four grounds of self-confidence, bears the ten powers, and is a bull among men, a lion among men, an elephant among men, a thoroughbred among men, a stallion among men; he possesses infinite knowledge and infinite splendor.

He is of infinite fame, wealthy, possessing great riches and treasures; he is a leader, a guide, an instructor, one who makes things known, one who inspires reflection, one who looks upon others, and one who inspires confidence.
For that Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path;
he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the skilled master of the path, and his disciples even now follow that path.
They dwell having subsequently attained [these qualities].

For that Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he has become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata.
There is nothing unknown, unseen, uncomprehended, unrealized, or untouched by wisdom for that Blessed One.
Taking the past, the future, and the present, all phenomena in every aspect come within the range of the vision of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Whatever is to be known, whatever phenomenon is to be understood—whether it be for one’s own benefit, for the benefit of others, or for the benefit of both;
whether it be a benefit pertaining to the present life or a benefit pertaining to the future life—[all such things come within his knowledge].
Whether the meaning is superficial or profound, hidden or concealed, implicit or explicit, blameless or stainless,
purified or ultimate— all that revolves within the Buddha’s knowledge.
Every bodily action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, follows after knowledge; every verbal action follows after knowledge; every mental action follows after knowledge.
The Buddha’s knowledge regarding the past is unobstructed; his knowledge regarding the future is unobstructed; his knowledge regarding the present is unobstructed.
To the extent that there is an object to be known, to that extent there is knowledge; to the extent that there is knowledge, to that extent there is an object to be known.
Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there a path of the knowable beyond knowledge.
These phenomena stand as mutual limits for one another.

Just as when two caskets are perfectly joined together, the lower casket does not overstep the upper one, and the upper casket does not overstep the lower one, but they stand with their limits meeting one another;
even so, for the Buddha, the Blessed One, the range of what is to be known (*neyya*) and his knowledge (*ñāṇa*) stand with their limits meeting one another:

as far as there is the range of what is to be known, so far extends his knowledge; as far as his knowledge extends, so far extends the range of what is to be known. It is bounded by the range of what is to be known.
Knowledge is the limit of the knowable; knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there a path of the knowable beyond knowledge.
These phenomena stand as mutual limits; regarding all phenomena, the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, proceeds.
All phenomena are dependent upon the Buddha, the Blessed One’s, advertence, dependent upon his desire, dependent upon his attention, and dependent upon the arising of his consciousness.

The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, extends toward all beings; and the Blessed One knows the disposition of all beings, he knows their latent tendencies, he knows their conduct, and he knows their inclinations.

He discerns beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust in their eyes, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those of good character and those of bad character, those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct, and those who are capable and those who are incapable.
The world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, revolves within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge.
Just as whatever fish and turtles there may be, even including the *timitimingala*, move about within the great ocean;
even so, the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its gods and humans, moves about within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge.
Just as whatever winged creatures there may be, even including the *garuḷa* Vainateyya, move about in some region of the sky;
In the same way, even those who are equal to Sāriputta in wisdom move only within a fraction of the Buddha’s knowledge.
The Buddha’s knowledge stands having pervaded and surpassed the wisdom of gods and humans.
Even those wise kṣatriyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics who are subtle and have completed their training in other doctrines [are likewise surpassed].
Like those who pierce a hair-tip, they move about as if splitting apart the various speculative views with the reach of their wisdom.
Having repeatedly formulated questions, they approach the Tathāgata and ask about matters that are hidden and concealed.
These questions, once explained and answered by the Blessed One, become clearly demonstrated with their underlying reasons.
And those who were cast down became equal to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One alone outshone them there by means of his wisdom:
"I have come together with the Shaken One; you will not be able to proceed with me."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Then you have come to a state of discursive thought,
contemplating various speculative views with the mind.”
“Dhona, you have met with your match;
indeed, you will not be able to proceed.
This concludes the eighth exposition, the Pasūra Sutta.
